381.t: Peggy Sue, Otis Blackwell's Presley demos and Bobby Darin
381.s: He played on Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue in New York, Otis Blackwell demos that Presley copied, and Bobby Darin's Splish Splash.
381.q: "The Buddy Holly Story," which everybody is raving about it. But nobody knows that he was recording down south or wherever he was, but his first big record, "Peggy Sue", was recorded in New York City and Dick Jacobs

381.t: Hit records: Platters, Brook Benton, Ray Charles and Colonel Bogie's March
381.s: He lists hits he drummed on, and how a snare on a timpani gave Mitch Miller a field-drum sound.
381.q: Then, I recorded, like all of the Platters records. I made "The Great Pretender", "Stardust", oh, let's see, "The Great Pretender", "Stardust", "Harbor Lights" -- in fact, everything that the Platters made with Tony Williams, I was playing drums on.

381.t: Perez Prado's Patricia and the invention of its overdubbed rhythm
381.s: He saved producer Herman Diaz's job by suggesting a rhythm for overdubbing onto Prado's tapes.
381.q: Then I did another record that sold almost two million records -- that was Perez Prado, a tune called "Patricia". That was another thing where they had these tapes that were recorded out in California, and the A&R man, who was Herman Diaz, was on the verge of losing his job, and so

381.t: Resume of studio hits: Four Seasons, Neil Sedaka, Connie Francis, Paul Anka
381.s: At Hinton's urging he lists hit sessions, including the first bass drum mike on What's the Matter, Baby.
381.q: Vince Martin was a folk singer. I can't remember the fellow's name; he's a movie actor now, but he was also a member of the group.

381.t: How Patricia was built on an overdub for Perez Prado
381.s: Retelling the tape-overdub story: a tambourine part, bass guitar and brushes made Patricia a near million-seller.
381.q: Right, the first overdub. There were these tapes sitting up on the shelf that Perez Prado had recorded out in California. So they brought the tapes in to New York to Herman Diez, who was the A+R man at the time at RCA.

381.t: Roy Hamilton and the cowbell on Love Is Strange
381.s: Jesse Stone arranged Don't Let Go; his cowbell suggestion completed Mickey and Sylvia's Love Is Strange.
381.q: And there was something that was lacking in the making of the record, in the record, and they didn't know what it was, so I suggested to let me play a cow bell. We played about four bars and we made the record, and it sold in the millions. Another hit record.

381.t: More hits: the Platters, Jackie Wilson, Brook Benton and the Fools Rush In rhythm
381.s: He lists more sessions and explains he took the Fools Rush In rhythm from hillbilly rhythm guitar.
381.q: Then I did "Jim Dandy" with Laverne Baker, I did "My Prayer" with the Platters, "Twilight Time," "Stardust," "Only You," "The Great Pretender," "Smoke Gets In Your Eyes" -- all of these were made with the Platters.

381.t: Dinah Washington's brushes and Ray Charles teaching a gospel feel
381.s: On What a Difference a Day Makes he used press rolls with brushes; Ray Charles showed him the church quarter-note brush feel for Drown in My Own Tears.
381.q: And then I did "What a Difference a Day Makes" with Dinah Washington. Now that was another one that everyone was talking about the rhythm, and the rhythm on that was the press rolls with the brushes -- that was what that was. Instead of playing like that with the sticks, I played with the brushes.…

381.t: The 12/8 rhythm on I Put a Spell on You and more hits
381.s: Screaming Jay Hawkins's record was the first R&B date using 12/8; he lists many more sessions with Joe Turner, Buddy Holly and others.
381.q: But that was the first time -- "I Put A Spell on You with Screaming Jay Hawkins. Then I did, "Where Are You" with Dinah Washington.

381.t: Arrangers, Clyde Otis and the rhythm section deciding the groove
381.s: They name the arrangers and Clyde Otis hits like Ramblin' Rose; Hinton says Francis led the rhythm section.
381.q: should have brought that thing -- I got a thing at home that I can bring with a whole list of names on that.

381.t: Clyde Otis demo sessions and Mercury
381.s: Hinton recalls Francis bringing him into Clyde Otis's demo group with Bedford Hendrix arrangements.
381.q: Oh, I really got into the recording business then.

267.t: Sessions behind Pee Wee Crayton, T-Bone Walker and Shirley and Lee
267.s: Ford recalls Imperial sessions with Tommy Ridgley, Pee Wee Crayton and T-Bone Walker, and Shirley and Lee's first record.
267.q: Yeah, Tommy Ridgely, Pee Wee Creighton. Oh, you did the Pee Wee Creighton? One of them for Imperial. That was supposed to be a very important session. T-Bone Walker. I remember one tune I had a solo, and I'd like to hear it now, you better go now, yours too. For T-Bone? No, it was Pee Wee…

323.t: Recording the albums and the piece 'Idyell'
323.s: Album session length, how Idyell grew from TV work, and the Henry Morgan spoofs.
323.q: Well a session was three hours. But an album, no, that took more than three hours. It might have taken us all day. But it was “More Than You Can Stand.” It’s a long LP. That’s where I play “Saxophobia.” And then he wrote a piece called “Idyell” but it wasn’t called anything. I’ll tell you what…

163.t: Record dates: 'Primrose Lane', 'The Big Hurt' and Capitol work
163.s: He recalls his hits, the Radio Recorders filter effect, rock and rhythm and blues calls, and 'Li'l Abner' with Nelson Riddle.
163.q: Well I think the only hit I was on was something Lane — “Primrose Lane.” And I think I faked an introduction on that, and they always say evidently whatever I did was good.
